transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
Democratic candidates are celebrating sweeping wins in the midterm elections
and will retake control of the House and Senate come January.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican State Attorney General Ken Paxton to win a Senate seat.
Talarico will be the first Democratic senator from Texas in more than 30 years.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al Syed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in that state Senate contest.
NPR's Sam Greenglass has more from Detroit.
This race for an open Senate seat currently held by Democrats was among the most closely watched in the nation.
A test of how an anti-establishment progressive would fare in a perennial Midwest battleground.
Now Al Syed will be the first Muslim American in the Senate.
After a bruising primary, uniting the party was rocky.
But the former public health official galvanized voters by harnessing anger over the cost of living and political corruption.
Al Syed heads to Congress promising to push Medicare for all and curb corporate money in politics.
Sam Greenglass, NPR News, Detroit.
Republican Democratic senator from Kansas in more than a century.
In Maine, longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins was defeated by Democrat Troy Jackson.
They're still counting the votes in Alaska's Senate race.
In the races for governor, Republican incumbent Greg Abbott lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in Texas.
Hinojosa will be the state's first Latina governor and the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than three decades.
In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has won the governor's race.
The former Atlanta mayor defeated Republican Rick Jackson to become the country's first black female governor.
In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become that state's next governor.
In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds won the governor's race.
He will be that state's first black governor.
The heavy election losses for Republicans are a rebuke of President Trump, who told voters leading up to election day to pretend his name was on the ballot.
He's speaking here to Fox News.
The Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard.
They were, you know, they've been fighting for a long time. They've been fighting me for a long time.
The president was speaking last night. This is NPR News.
Voters in Washington, D.C. have elected Democrat Robert White to succeed Eleanor Holmes Norton as the city's non-voting delegate to Congress.
White's win marks a new era in D.C. politics, as Matt Blitz with member station WAMU reports.
The former D.C. council member defeated two other candidates in the race to replace civil rights icon Eleanor Holmes Norton,
who announced a retirement after serving for more than three decades.
White's win is set to make him only the third ever D.C. delegate since the office was established in 1970.
In his victory speech, White spoke of bringing jobs back to the city hit hard by the Trump administration's federal cuts and the urgent need for D.C. statehood.
We are now the last democracy on Earth that denies full participation from the residents of its capital city. This is wrong. It must end and it will end here.
White is set to be sworn into Congress on January 3rd. For NPR News, I'm Matt Blitz in Washington.
In other news, the National Transportation Safety Board says a piece from the Learjet that crashed in South Florida on Sunday was found nearly four miles from the crash site.
The NTSB says the discovery confirms the private jet was breaking apart before it hit the ground outside West Palm Beach, killing all nine people aboard.
Investigators say most of the left elevator from the jet's tail section was found in three pieces. Federal investigators say weather is also being looked at.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.
